1	# Drive Upload — Step 6: Upload queue (UI/UX plan)
2	
3	Scope: UI/UX only. Backend wiring (an App RPC around the existing `drive.UploadFile`,
4	any progress plumbing) is a separate, later concern.
5	
6	## Per-file state model
7	
8	New hook, `useUploadQueue`, lifted in `DriveUploadMode` alongside `useFileTree` /
9	`useDriveAssignments`. Tracks a status per `LocalFile.path`:
10	
11	- `idle` — no run has touched this file yet
12	- `queued` — a run has started; waiting its turn
13	- `uploading` — actively transferring
14	- `done` — succeeded
15	- `error` — failed, carries an error message
16	
17	A group's status is never stored directly — it's derived by rolling up its files'
18	statuses (recursively through subgroups), the same way effective Drive-folder
19	assignment is already resolved by walking down from the group.
20	
21	## Concurrency
22	
23	Sequential worker (concurrency = 1) for the first version: one file `uploading` at a
24	time, others sit `queued` in tree order. The status model above is concurrency-agnostic
25	— bumping to an N-way pool later is a scheduler change only, not a UI redesign.
26	
27	## Prerequisite: toolbar layout
28	
29	`DriveUploadMode` doesn't have a toolbar today — `ResizableLeftPanel` is the whole
30	body, and the root-folder picker (`ClippedPath`) lives inline at the top of the left
31	panel. Before step 6, add a toolbar strip spanning the full width above the
32	three-column layout, structurally matching the `Box` + `Group` toolbar already used in
33	`SplitMode`/`MergeMode`, and move the root-folder picker into it (left-aligned).
34	`Upload All` will land in this same toolbar (right-aligned) once step 6 builds it.
35	This is a pure layout move — no behavior change to `pickRoot`/`useFileTree`.
36	
37	## Upload All button
38	
39	Location: the toolbar from the prerequisite step above, right-aligned — matching
40	where Merge & Save (`MergeMode`) and Export (`SplitMode`) already sit, rather than the
41	bottom of the left panel as sketched in spec.md's current mockup.
42	
43	There's no "run in progress" state for the button itself: the moment a run starts,
44	the modal opens and its overlay sits on top of the toolbar, blocking and dimming it
45	(same as everything else behind it). Whatever the button displayed right before the
46	click is inert and hidden under the overlay for the duration of the run. The button
47	only needs two states:
48	
49	- **Nothing uploaded yet (or nothing left to retry)** — label "Upload All". Disabled
50	  (with a tooltip explaining why) until every file in the tree resolves to an
51	  effective Drive assignment (own or inherited from a group). Clicking starts a run
52	  over every file and opens the upload modal.
53	- **Run finished, some files failed** — label "Retry Failed (2)", enabled. Clicking
54	  reopens the modal and re-queues only the `error` files — it does not re-touch files
55	  that are already `done`.
56	-- **Run finished, everything succeeded**: nothing left to upload, so re-running
57	would create duplicates on Drive — disabled, label "All Uploaded".
58	
59	## Left panel becomes read-only
60	
61	Once "Upload All" is clicked for the first time, the entire file tree becomes
62	read-only for the rest of that tree's session — not just while the modal is open, but
63	after it closes too, regardless of whether a given file ended up `done`, `error`, or
64	was never attempted. This covers every `DriveAssignmentField` badge (group-level and
65	file-level), and, once inline renaming (step 4) exists, the filename inputs as well.
66	Retry always re-sends to the same locked-in destination and name. The only way out of
67	read-only is picking a new root folder, which discards the whole tree and upload-queue
68	state and starts fresh.
69	
70	This avoids having to reconcile "the user changed the destination or name of a file
71	that already uploaded" — it simply can't happen.
72	
73	## Upload modal
74	
75	Rather than showing live progress inline in the main tree — which would require
76	individually disabling the root-folder picker, every assignment badge, inline rename
77	inputs, and the mode tab bar in `App.tsx` — the upload run owns a dedicated modal
78	(same `Modal` component/pattern as the Split-mode success modal).
79	
80	Mantine's `Modal` renders a full-viewport overlay and traps focus by default, so it
81	blocks interaction with everything behind it (tree, root picker, tab bar) with no
82	extra plumbing into those components. While a run is active:
83	
84	- `closeOnClickOutside={false}`, `closeOnEscape={false}`, no close button.
85	- A **"Cancel remaining"** action in the footer: stops starting new files (does not
86	  abort an in-flight request), letting the user close once the current file resolves.
87	
88	Content: a read-only rendering of the group/file tree (no collapsing, no assignment
89	badges, no click-to-preview — simpler than reusing `GroupNode`/`FileList` as-is, so
90	this is a small dedicated component built for the modal).
91	
92	- **File row**: name + status —
93	  - `queued` — dimmed "Queued"
94	  - `uploading` — `Loader size="xs"` + "Uploading…"
95	  - `done` — green ✓ + "Uploaded"
96	  - `error` — red ⚠ + error message + inline **Retry** button (re-queues just that
97	    file, doesn't affect others or restart the batch)
98	- **Group header**: rollup count while in progress (e.g. "3/5").
99	
100	Progress is indeterminate (spinner, not a percentage bar) since Drive's simple upload
101	doesn't give byte-level progress without resumable upload.
102	
103	"Close" is disabled while anything is `queued`/`uploading`; becomes available once the
104	run reaches a terminal rest state (success or with failures still showing Retry).
105	
106	## After the modal closes
107	
108	Upload-queue state persists past the close (it's lifted in `DriveUploadMode`, not
109	modal-local), so the main tree reflects the last run:
110	
111	- `GroupNode` header shows an **"Open in Drive"** link (opens the group's assigned
112	  Drive folder) in place of the assignment badge/rollup, once every file in that group
113	  is `done`.
114	- `FileList` rows get a small terminal ✓/⚠ badge next to the size/page-count line for
115	  files that were part of the last run.
116	- "Upload All" reflects the state machine above ("Retry Failed (N)" / "All Uploaded").
117	
118	## Implementation notes
119	
120	- **Shared tree-traversal utility.** Three consumers need to walk the same
121	  `LocalFileGroup` recursion: the sequential worker (needs a flat, ordered file list
122	  to know what to upload next), the modal's per-group rollup counts, and the
123	  "every file in this group is `done`" check driving the Open-in-Drive link. Write one
124	  function (e.g. `flattenFiles(group): LocalFile[]`) that all three consume, rather
125	  than three independent recursive walks over `subgroups` that could drift out of sync
126	  with each other's handling of nesting.
127	- **Backend RPC.** `drive.UploadFile(ctx, localPath, folderID)` exists as a Go function
128	  but has no Wails App-level RPC wrapper yet — 6a needs to add one (bindings will
129	  regenerate via Wails, don't hand-edit `frontend/wailsjs/`). Give it a `name`
130	  parameter (defaulting to `filepath.Base(localPath)`, unused until step 4 wires up
131	  inline renaming) so the signature doesn't need to change again once renaming lands.
132	
133	## Explicitly out of scope for this step
134	
135	- Conflict-check UI before upload — step 9.
136	- Post-upload delete/archive prompt — step 8.
137	- Recently-used folders list, batch (multi-select) assignment, inline renaming — steps
138	  3c, 3e, 4, tracked separately.
139	- Byte-level upload progress.
140	
141	## Suggested checklist breakdown (for spec.md)
142	
143	- **Prerequisite**: add the toolbar strip; move the root-folder picker into it.
144	- **6a**: `useUploadQueue` state model + sequential worker (no UI yet).
145	- **6b**: Upload modal — tree rendering, per-file/per-group status, Retry, Cancel
146	  remaining, blocking close behavior.
147	- **6c**: Post-run residual state in the main tree — terminal badges, "Open in Drive"
148	  links, Upload All button state machine, read-only lock on the file tree.

# Drive Upload — Step 6: Upload queue (UI/UX plan)

Scope: UI/UX only. Backend wiring (an App RPC around the existing `drive.UploadFile`,
any progress plumbing) is a separate, later concern.

## Per-file state model

New hook, `useUploadQueue`, lifted in `DriveUploadMode` alongside `useFileTree` /
`useDriveAssignments`. Tracks a status per `LocalFile.path`:

- `idle` — no run has touched this file yet
- `queued` — a run has started; waiting its turn
- `uploading` — actively transferring
- `done` — succeeded
- `error` — failed, carries an error message

A group's status is never stored directly — it's derived by rolling up its files'
statuses (recursively through subgroups), the same way effective Drive-folder
assignment is already resolved by walking down from the group.

## Concurrency

Sequential worker (concurrency = 1) for the first version: one file `uploading` at a
time, others sit `queued` in tree order. The status model above is concurrency-agnostic
— bumping to an N-way pool later is a scheduler change only, not a UI redesign.

## Prerequisite: toolbar layout

`DriveUploadMode` doesn't have a toolbar today — `ResizableLeftPanel` is the whole
body, and the root-folder picker (`ClippedPath`) lives inline at the top of the left
panel. Before step 6, add a toolbar strip spanning the full width above the
three-column layout, structurally matching the `Box` + `Group` toolbar already used in
`SplitMode`/`MergeMode`, and move the root-folder picker into it (left-aligned).
`Upload All` will land in this same toolbar (right-aligned) once step 6 builds it.
This is a pure layout move — no behavior change to `pickRoot`/`useFileTree`.

## Upload All button

Location: the toolbar from the prerequisite step above, right-aligned — matching
where Merge & Save (`MergeMode`) and Export (`SplitMode`) already sit, rather than the
bottom of the left panel as sketched in spec.md's current mockup.

There's no "run in progress" state for the button itself: the moment a run starts,
the modal opens and its overlay sits on top of the toolbar, blocking and dimming it
(same as everything else behind it). Whatever the button displayed right before the
click is inert and hidden under the overlay for the duration of the run. The button
only needs two states:

- **Nothing uploaded yet (or nothing left to retry)** — label "Upload All". Disabled
  (with a tooltip explaining why) until every file in the tree resolves to an
  effective Drive assignment (own or inherited from a group). Clicking starts a run
  over every file and opens the upload modal.
- **Run finished, some files failed** — label "Retry Failed (2)", enabled. Clicking
  reopens the modal and re-queues only the `error` files — it does not re-touch files
  that are already `done`.
-- **Run finished, everything succeeded**: nothing left to upload, so re-running
would create duplicates on Drive — disabled, label "All Uploaded".

## Left panel becomes read-only

Once "Upload All" is clicked for the first time, the entire file tree becomes
read-only for the rest of that tree's session — not just while the modal is open, but
after it closes too, regardless of whether a given file ended up `done`, `error`, or
was never attempted. This covers every `DriveAssignmentField` badge (group-level and
file-level), and, once inline renaming (step 4) exists, the filename inputs as well.
Retry always re-sends to the same locked-in destination and name. The only way out of
read-only is picking a new root folder, which discards the whole tree and upload-queue
state and starts fresh.

This avoids having to reconcile "the user changed the destination or name of a file
that already uploaded" — it simply can't happen.

## Upload modal

Rather than showing live progress inline in the main tree — which would require
individually disabling the root-folder picker, every assignment badge, inline rename
inputs, and the mode tab bar in `App.tsx` — the upload run owns a dedicated modal
(same `Modal` component/pattern as the Split-mode success modal).

Mantine's `Modal` renders a full-viewport overlay and traps focus by default, so it
blocks interaction with everything behind it (tree, root picker, tab bar) with no
extra plumbing into those components. While a run is active:

- `closeOnClickOutside={false}`, `closeOnEscape={false}`, no close button.
- A **"Cancel remaining"** action in the footer: stops starting new files (does not
  abort an in-flight request), letting the user close once the current file resolves.

Content: a read-only rendering of the group/file tree (no collapsing, no assignment
badges, no click-to-preview — simpler than reusing `GroupNode`/`FileList` as-is, so
this is a small dedicated component built for the modal).

- **File row**: name + status —
  - `queued` — dimmed "Queued"
  - `uploading` — `Loader size="xs"` + "Uploading…"
  - `done` — green ✓ + "Uploaded"
  - `error` — red ⚠ + error message + inline **Retry** button (re-queues just that
    file, doesn't affect others or restart the batch)
- **Group header**: rollup count while in progress (e.g. "3/5").

Progress is indeterminate (spinner, not a percentage bar) since Drive's simple upload
doesn't give byte-level progress without resumable upload.

"Close" is disabled while anything is `queued`/`uploading`; becomes available once the
run reaches a terminal rest state (success or with failures still showing Retry).

## After the modal closes

Upload-queue state persists past the close (it's lifted in `DriveUploadMode`, not
modal-local), so the main tree reflects the last run:

- `GroupNode` header shows an **"Open in Drive"** link (opens the group's assigned
  Drive folder) in place of the assignment badge/rollup, once every file in that group
  is `done`.
- `FileList` rows get a small terminal ✓/⚠ badge next to the size/page-count line for
  files that were part of the last run.
- "Upload All" reflects the state machine above ("Retry Failed (N)" / "All Uploaded").

## Implementation notes

- **Shared tree-traversal utility.** Three consumers need to walk the same
  `LocalFileGroup` recursion: the sequential worker (needs a flat, ordered file list
  to know what to upload next), the modal's per-group rollup counts, and the
  "every file in this group is `done`" check driving the Open-in-Drive link. Write one
  function (e.g. `flattenFiles(group): LocalFile[]`) that all three consume, rather
  than three independent recursive walks over `subgroups` that could drift out of sync
  with each other's handling of nesting.
- **Backend RPC.** `drive.UploadFile(ctx, localPath, folderID)` exists as a Go function
  but has no Wails App-level RPC wrapper yet — 6a needs to add one (bindings will
  regenerate via Wails, don't hand-edit `frontend/wailsjs/`). Give it a `name`
  parameter (defaulting to `filepath.Base(localPath)`, unused until step 4 wires up
  inline renaming) so the signature doesn't need to change again once renaming lands.

## Explicitly out of scope for this step

- Conflict-check UI before upload — step 9.
- Post-upload delete/archive prompt — step 8.
- Recently-used folders list, batch (multi-select) assignment, inline renaming — steps
  3c, 3e, 4, tracked separately.
- Byte-level upload progress.

## Suggested checklist breakdown (for spec.md)

- **Prerequisite**: add the toolbar strip; move the root-folder picker into it.
- **6a**: `useUploadQueue` state model + sequential worker (no UI yet).
- **6b**: Upload modal — tree rendering, per-file/per-group status, Retry, Cancel
  remaining, blocking close behavior.
- **6c**: Post-run residual state in the main tree — terminal badges, "Open in Drive"

3:A desktop application for post-processing PDF files containing batches of scanned documents. The app has three modes: **Merge**, **Split**, and **Drive Upload**.
4-
5-## Tech stack
6-
7-- **Desktop framework**: Wails
8-- **Backend**: Go
9-- **Frontend**: TypeScript + React
10-- **UI components**: Mantine
11-- **Virtualization**: TanStack Virtual
12-- **Drag-and-drop**: dnd-kit
13-- **PDF manipulation**: pdfcpu
14-- **PDF rendering** (thumbnails): `pdftoppm` (Poppler, system install, called as subprocess)
15-
16-## Common elements
17-
18-Both modes include a thumbnail panel and a page detail panel, and support the same per-page editing operations.
19-
20-### Thumbnail panel
21-
22-A vertically scrolling strip of page thumbnails. Width is user-adjustable via a drag handle; thumbnails scale to fill the panel width. Rendering is on-demand and virtualized — only visible thumbnails (plus a small overscan buffer) are rendered at any given time.
23-
24-The Go backend exposes a per-page render method returning a base64-encoded PNG; the frontend requests thumbnails as they scroll into view (`pdftoppm` subprocess).
25-
26-#### Keyboard shortcuts
27-
28-| Key                    | Action                                     |
29-| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
30-| `R`                    | Rotate selected page clockwise 90°         |
31-| `Shift+R`              | Rotate selected page counter-clockwise 90° |
32-| `Delete` / `Backspace` | Toggle skip on the selected page           |
33-| `←` / `→`              | Select previous / next page                |
34-
35-### Page detail panel
36-
37-Shows the currently selected page at reading resolution. Selecting a thumbnail updates it.
38-
39-Supports:
40-
41-- **Pan**: drag to pan.
42-- **Zoom**: scroll wheel or trackpad pinch to zoom in/out.
43-- **Navigate**: `←` / `→` to move to the previous/next page.
44-
45-Implemented with `react-zoom-pan-pinch`.
46-
47-### Page editing
48-
49-Individual pages can be edited in both modes before export or merge:
50-
51-- **Rotation**: pages can be rotated in 90° increments (clockwise or counter-clockwise).
52-- **Skip**: pages can be marked as skipped — excluded from the output but remaining visible in the thumbnail view (greyed out). A page is skipped by clicking a skip icon that appears on hover, or via keyboard shortcut.
53-- **Reorder**: pages can be reordered by dragging thumbnails to a new position.
54-
55-## Mode: Merge
56-
57-For scanners that can only scan one side at a time. The user scans all front pages as one PDF and all back pages as another, then uses Merge mode to interleave them into a single PDF.
58-
59-### Workflow
60-
61-1. The user loads two PDF files, labelled **File A** and **File B**.
62-2. The user selects which file contains the first page (**First page in: File A / File B**).
63-3. A **Reverse File B** checkbox controls whether File B is reversed before interleaving. This should be checked when the paper stack was flipped between scans (the typical case, when scanning one side at a time), causing the second-scanned pages to be in reverse order.
64-4. The app interleaves the pages: A1, B1, A2, B2, etc.
65-5. The user saves the merged result as a new PDF file on disk.
66-
67-The merged PDF can then be opened in Split mode for further processing.
68-
69-### Unequal page counts
70-

168:For filing batches of local files (PDFs and other scans, e.g. images) to Google Drive. Intended as the step after Split mode: once PDFs are exported to a local folder, the user switches to Drive Upload to route each file (or subfolder of files) to the correct place in Drive.

172:1. The user enters Drive Upload mode. If arriving via the Split mode export success modal, the root local folder is pre-set to the Split output folder; otherwise the user picks a root folder.

=== feedback_separate_commits ===
---
name: feedback-separate-commits
description: "Don't mix cleanups with feature code — point them out first, commit them immediately, before starting feature work"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 1b7f78a3-a75a-48b1-be75-47ffc0b70a3f
---

Before writing feature code, if there's cleanup to do (unused props, dead code, a component that should move to a shared location, etc.), point it out and ask whether to clean up first. If yes, apply the cleanup and **commit it right away** — don't just stage it and leave it sitting uncommitted until the feature work is also done.

**Why:** User wants a clean git history where each commit does one thing. Confirmed again on 2026-07-02: during Drive Upload mode Step 2, I staged a cleanup (moving `ClippedPath.tsx` to a shared components dir) at the start but didn't commit it until asked at the very end, by which point it was sitting alongside unrelated staged/unstaged feature changes. The user wants the commit created immediately after the cleanup is applied, not batched. This is about commit *sequencing* with this user, not a rule about resulting repo content, so it lives in memory rather than CLAUDE.md — see [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].

**How to apply:** When starting a feature, scan the files to be modified for unused/dead code or things that should move/get extracted. If found, mention it before writing any feature code. Once agreed, apply the cleanup and commit it immediately with its own descriptive message — before writing a single line of the actual feature. Then proceed to feature work as separate, later commit(s).

=== feedback_commit_confirmation ===
---
name: feedback-commit-confirmation
description: "Never commit without the user's explicit confirmation on that turn; show the draft commit message before running git commit; use git commit -F <file> -- <paths>"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 1b7f78a3-a75a-48b1-be75-47ffc0b70a3f
---

Never run `git commit` unless the user has explicitly asked for it in this turn. An earlier "commit" instruction does not authorize committing again later in the session — each commit (or batch of commits for one piece of work) needs its own explicit go-ahead. After finishing a reviewable chunk of work, stop and ask whether to commit; don't just do it because that's the rhythm the conversation fell into.

**Why:** User corrected this on 2026-07-02: after saying "commit" once (for Step 2 work), I kept committing on my own for subsequent steps (Step 3a, a test-infra fix, Step 3b) without being asked again each time. This is about the approval relationship with this specific user — a different user of this repo might not want that friction at all — so it belongs in memory, not CLAUDE.md. See [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].

**How to apply:** Finish the work, run verification (build/test/typecheck), summarize what changed, and explicitly ask "want me to commit this?" — then wait. Do not commit proactively even if the previous turn's work was committed after a similar request. This applies within a single session and especially across multiple pieces of work in a row (e.g. a multi-step checklist implementation) — each step's commit needs its own confirmation, not just the first one. See also [[feedback_separate_commits]] for how to split what does get committed once confirmed.

**Show the commit message first (added 2026-07-08):** Even once the user says "commit," show the drafted commit message in the chat turn first, then commit (in that same turn, no extra round-trip needed unless the user objects to the message). Why: user asked to see the message before it's used, so they can review/edit wording before it lands in history.

**Use `git commit -F <file>`, not inline `-m "$(cat <<'EOF' ...)"` (added 2026-07-10):** Draft the message, write it to a scratchpad file with the Write tool, show its contents in chat as the preview, then run `git commit -F <path>`. Why: passing the message inline via a heredoc broke repeatedly whenever the message contained an apostrophe (`picker's`, `it's`) — something outside my own command also wraps the whole shell invocation in single quotes (likely a logging/sandboxing layer doing `eval '<command>'`), and a literal apostrophe anywhere in the text prematurely closes that outer quoting since single quotes can't be escaped from within themselves. Writing the message to a file sidesteps shell quoting entirely — apostrophes, quotes, backticks are all safe in file content. `-F` also naturally satisfies the "show the message first" rule above, since the file is written (and can be shown) before the commit runs. This is purely a workaround for how *I* invoke shell commands in this sandboxed environment — not relevant to a human contributor or a rule about repo content — so it's memory, not CLAUDE.md.

**Skip `git status` / `git add`, pass pathspecs straight to `git commit` (added 2026-07-10):** Default commit command is now `git commit -F <message-file> -- <path1> <path2> ...`, listing exactly the files touched this turn. `git commit <pathspec>` stages and commits only those paths' current working-tree content, regardless of what else is dirty elsewhere — no preceding `git add` needed. `git status` is skippable too since I already know which files I edited from my own tool calls this session; I don't need to discover that via status. Why: user asked for a leaner commit flow after watching the status→add→commit dance every time. Caveat: this repo has had stray unrelated modified files show up before (e.g. `frontend/wailsjs/runtime/*` regenerated by a `wails dev` run outside the session) — always naming explicit paths on `git commit` is what keeps those out, so don't switch to `git commit -a` or `git add -A` even though they'd also skip the status/add dance.

=== feedback_warn_large_diffs ===
---
name: feedback-warn-large-diffs
description: "Proactively warn before implementing any request (chat or spec.md) that looks like it'll produce a large/churned diff, and propose splitting it"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 1b7f78a3-a75a-48b1-be75-47ffc0b70a3f
---

Before starting implementation on a requested feature or change — whether it comes from a spec.md checklist item or an ad-hoc chat message — assess whether it looks like it will touch many files or produce a large diff. If so, flag this to the user up front and propose splitting the work into smaller, independently reviewable steps (see CLAUDE.md's "break checklist work into small steps" convention for the 1a/1b/1c naming) before writing code.

**Why:** User confirmed on 2026-07-08 that this proactive warning should apply universally, not just when authoring spec.md checklist items — any chat request that would churn a lot of code should get the same treatment. This is a personal workflow preference (a checkpoint on *when* I pause to confirm with the user), not an objective repo convention, so it lives in memory rather than CLAUDE.md — see [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].

**How to apply:** Do this assessment for every non-trivial implementation request, regardless of source (spec checklist or plain chat ask). Give the warning before writing code, not after. Trivial/small requests don't need this treatment — use judgment on what counts as "large."

Run `npm run tsc` from the `./frontend` directory (not `npx tsc --noEmit`).

**Why:** The project has a `tsc` script in package.json; the correct invocation is `npm run tsc` inside `frontend/`.

**How to apply:** Always use this command when verifying TypeScript correctness for frontend changes.

Do not attempt to launch `wails dev`, search for the wails binary, or take screenshots of the app to verify UI changes. The user will test manually.

**How to apply:** After implementing UI changes, do a TypeScript type-check (`npx tsc --noEmit`) to verify correctness, then report the implementation as done. Do not try to launch the app or take screenshots.

Why: passing the message inline via a heredoc broke repeatedly whenever the message contained an apostrophe (`picker's`, `it's`) — something outside my own command also wraps the whole shell invocation in single quotes (likely a logging/sandboxing layer doing `eval '<command>'`), and a literal apostrophe anywhere in the text prematurely closes that outer quoting since single quotes can't be escaped from within themselves. Writing the message to a file sidesteps shell quoting entirely — apostrophes, quotes, backticks are all safe in file content. `-F` also naturally satisfies the "show the message first" rule above, since the file is written (and can be shown) before the commit runs. This is purely a workaround for how *I* invoke shell commands in this sandboxed environment — not relevant to a human contributor or a rule about repo content — so it's memory, not CLAUDE.md.

**Skip `git status` / `git add`, pass pathspecs straight to `git commit` (added 2026-07-10):** Default commit command is now `git commit -F <message-file> -- <path1> <path2> ...`, listing exactly the files touched this turn. `git commit <pathspec>` stages and commits only those paths' current working-tree content, regardless of what else is dirty elsewhere — no preceding `git add` needed. `git status` is skippable too since I already know which files I edited from my own tool calls this session; I don't need to discover that via status. Why: user asked for a leaner commit flow after watching the status→add→commit dance every time. Caveat: this repo has had stray unrelated modified files show up before (e.g. `frontend/wailsjs/runtime/*` regenerated by a `wails dev` run outside the session) — always naming explicit paths on `git commit` is what keeps those out, so don't switch to `git commit -a` or `git add -A` even though they'd also skip the status/add dance.

12	// UploadFile uploads the local file at localPath to the Drive folder with
13	// the given ID. The filename on Drive matches the base name of localPath.
14	// Returns the ID of the created Drive file.
15	func UploadFile(ctx context.Context, localPath, folderID string) (string, error) {
16		f, err := os.Open(localPath)
17		if err != nil {
18			return "", fmt.Errorf("open %s: %w", localPath, err)
19		}
20		defer f.Close()
21	
22		svc, err := service(ctx)
23		if err != nil {
24			return "", err
25		}
26	
27		meta := &drive.File{
28			Name:    filepath.Base(localPath),
29			Parents: []string{folderID},
30		}
31		created, err := svc.Files.Create(meta).Media(f).Fields("id, name, size").Do()
32		if err != nil {
33			return "", fmt.Errorf("upload %s: %w", localPath, err)
34		}
35		return created.Id, nil
36	}

13	  groupAssignments: Map<string, DriveAssignment>

15	  setGroupAssignment: (groupKey: string, assignment: DriveAssignment) => void

21	// Tracks Drive folder assignments made directly on a subfolder group or on
22	// an individual file (a file-level assignment overrides its group's).
23	// Resolving the *effective* assignment for a given group/file (own, else
24	// inherited from the nearest ancestor group, else none) is the caller's
25	// job, since only the caller knows the tree structure to walk.
26	export function useDriveAssignments(): DriveAssignmentsHandle {
27	  const [groupAssignments, setGroupAssignments] = useState<Map<string, DriveAssignment>>(new Map())
28	  const [fileOverrides, setFileOverrides] = useState<Map<string, DriveAssignment>>(new Map())
29	
30	  const setGroupAssignment = useCallback((groupKey: string, assignment: DriveAssignment) => {
31	    setGroupAssignments(prev => new Map(prev).set(groupKey, assignment))
32	  }, [])
33	
34	  const clearGroupAssignment = useCallback((groupKey: string) => {
35	    setGroupAssignments(prev => {
36	      const next = new Map(prev)
37	      next.delete(groupKey)
38	      return next
39	    })
40	  }, [])
41	
42	  const setFileOverride = useCallback((filePath: string, assignment: DriveAssignment) => {
43	    setFileOverrides(prev => new Map(prev).set(filePath, assignment))

47	    setFileOverrides(prev => {
48	      const next = new Map(prev)
49	      next.delete(filePath)
50	      return next
51	    })
52	  }, [])
53	
54	  return { groupAssignments, fileOverrides, setGroupAssignment, clearGroupAssignment, setFileOverride, clearFileOverride }
55	}

lastPrompt: The frontend will always pass a file name for the upload, even if it wasn't renamed, right?

content.text:
Yes — good thing to pin down now. Looking at the backend (`backend/filetree/filetree.go:16`), `LocalFile.Name` is documented as "filename including extension" and is set directly from the scanned directory entry (`entryName`), which is also what `file.path`'s basename is built from. So today, before inline renaming exists, `file.name` and `filepath.Base(file.path)` are always identical.

So the plan for 6c is: when building each `UploadJob`, pass `name: file.name` unconditionally — not empty string. That already equals what the backend's `name == "" → filepath.Base(localPath)` fallback would compute anyway, so the fallback is effectively unexercised by the app today (it'll matter once Step 4 lets `file.name`-equivalent diverge from the local filename). This matches the spec's phrasing that the `name` param is "unused until step 4" — the *fallback path* is unused, not the field itself.

One thing worth double-checking: my test fixtures in `index.test.tsx` (e.g. `{ path: '/root/misc.pdf', name: 'misc', ... }`) use a `name` without the extension, which doesn't match real backend output. That's a pre-existing simplification in that test file (not something I introduced), harmless for what those tests assert, but worth knowing it's not representative of production `name` values. I won't touch it unless you want it cleaned up.

message.content: what's the reason for all those useRef`s in useUploadQueue?

content.text:
Each one exists because `runQueue`'s `while` loop is a single long-lived async closure spanning multiple `await`s — and React state captured in a closure is frozen at the render it was read from, not "live." A `useState` value read inside that loop would never see updates made after the loop started running. Refs are the escape hatch: mutable, synchronously read/written, immune to render/closure staleness.

- **`jobsRef`** — job details (`folderId`/`name`) keyed by path, so the loop can look up a job's destination when it dequeues just its path. Doesn't drive rendering, so no reason for it to be state.
- **`pendingRef`** — the actual FIFO queue. Multiple `enqueue()` calls (e.g. `start()` then a `retry()` moments later) need to push onto the *same* live array the running loop is reading — if this were state, each push would be an async/batched update the in-flight loop wouldn't observe until its next render, which never happens since the loop itself isn't a component.
- **`runningRef`** — a synchronous mutex so two `enqueue()` calls in quick succession can't both see "not running" and spin up two overlapping loops both calling `shift()`. Needs a synchronous check-then-set; state's read/write isn't atomic across two rapid calls in the same tick.
- **`cancelledRef`** — checked every loop iteration; `cancelRemaining()` needs to flip it and have the *already-running* loop notice on its very next check, not on some future render.
- **`genRef`** — same idea, for `reset()`: bumped so a job that was already mid-`await` when reset happened can tell, once it resolves, that its run was invalidated and skip writing a stale status back into the (now-cleared) map.

`statuses` is the one piece of real `useState`, since that's the only thing that actually needs to trigger a re-render — everything else is bookkeeping the async loop needs to read/write synchronously between awaits.

message.content: Would it make sense to use useEffectEvent() instead of refs? Don't touch the code,just answer.

content.text:
No — `useEffectEvent` solves a different problem than what these refs are for, and its usage rules don't even fit how this hook is invoked.

`useEffectEvent` exists to let a `useEffect` read the *latest* reactive state/props without listing them as dependencies (avoiding stale closures inside an Effect, and avoiding needlessly re-running/re-subscribing the Effect when those values change). Critically, per its rules, an Effect Event can only be called from inside an Effect (or from another Effect Event called by one) — never from a plain event handler.

Nothing in `useUploadQueue` runs inside a `useEffect`. `start`/`retry`/`cancelRemaining`/`reset` are plain callbacks invoked directly from UI event handlers, and `runQueue` is a self-contained async function they kick off — there's no Effect for an Effect Event to be scoped to.

More fundamentally, the refs here aren't standing in for "read latest state" — they're the actual mutable storage: `pendingRef` is a live FIFO array multiple calls push onto and the loop shifts from; `jobsRef` is a lookup map; `runningRef`/`cancelledRef`/`genRef` are flags/counters mutated and checked synchronously between `await`s. `useEffectEvent` doesn't give you a place to store data across renders — it only wraps a function body so it sees current values of state/props that are stored elsewhere. Even if this were restructured to live inside an Effect, you'd still need refs (or state) underneath to hold the queue, the jobs map, and the counters; `useEffectEvent` wouldn't remove them.

message.content: The queue is basically a singleton, right? Doesn't it make sense to have an actual singleton, rather than trying to squeeze it into Reacts hook-logic?

content.text:
Not really, and here's why: it's only safe to treat as hook-scoped because the modal fully blocks the mode-tab bar for the entire duration a run is in flight (per the spec: "Mantine's Modal... blocks interaction with everything behind it... including the tab bar"). Since `DriveUploadMode` unmounts when you switch tabs (`{mode === 'drive' && <DriveUploadMode />}` in `App.tsx`), the only way this hook's in-flight state could get orphaned by an unmount is if navigation were possible mid-run — and the modal's overlay specifically prevents that. By the time the modal can be closed, nothing is `queued`/`uploading` anymore, so there's nothing left to lose.

A true module-level singleton would only earn its keep if uploads needed to survive a tab switch or be visible from multiple components — neither is true here — and it'd cost real complexity: you'd need `useSyncExternalStore` (or similar) to make React re-render on external mutations, and tests would need explicit teardown to avoid state leaking between cases (right now `renderHook` gives each test a fresh instance for free, which is why `useUploadQueue.test.ts` doesn't need any cleanup between tests). So the ref-based hook isn't a workaround — it's already the right shape given the constraint the spec deliberately built in.

8	// request overwrites the value, which lets the stale lower-res .then know it was superseded.
9	// failed tracks the highest width that failed per page; retries at higher widths are still allowed.
10	const entries = new Map<string, Entry>()
11	const loading = new Map<string, number>()
12	const failed = new Map<string, number>()
13	const listeners = new Set<() => void>()
14	
15	const pageKey = (path: string, page: number) => `${path}\0${page}`
16	
17	function notify() {
18	  for (const fn of listeners) fn()
19	}
20	
21	export function subscribe(fn: () => void): () => void {
22	  listeners.add(fn)
23	  return () => listeners.delete(fn)
24	}
25	
26	export function usePageCacheRender() {
27	  const [, setTick] = useState(0)
28	  useEffect(() => subscribe(() => setTick(t => t + 1)), [])
29	}
30	
31	export function getSrc(path: string, page: number): string | undefined {
32	  return entries.get(pageKey(path, page))?.src
33	}
34	
35	export function getCachedWidth(path: string, page: number): number | undefined {
36	  return entries.get(pageKey(path, page))?.width
37	}
38	
39	export function isLoading(path: string, page: number): boolean {
40	  return loading.has(pageKey(path, page))
41	}
42	
43	export function isFailed(path: string, page: number): boolean {
44	  return failed.has(pageKey(path, page))
45	}
46	
47	export function load(path: string, page: number, width: number): void {
48	  if (!path) return
49	  const k = pageKey(path, page)
50	  const existing = entries.get(k)
51	  if (existing && existing.width >= width) return
52	  const currentlyLoading = loading.get(k)
53	  // Don't start a new render if a higher-res one is already in-flight — it will supersede this one.
54	  if (currentlyLoading !== undefined && currentlyLoading >= width) return
55	  const failedAt = failed.get(k)
56	  if (failedAt !== undefined && failedAt >= width) return
57	  // Overwrite any lower-res in-flight entry. The superseded render will still complete but its
58	  // .then/.catch checks loading.get(k) === width before mutating state, so it becomes a no-op.
59	  loading.set(k, width)

61	    .then((b64) => {
62	      // A higher-res render may have completed while this one was in-flight — don't downgrade.
63	      const current = entries.get(k)
64	      if (!current || current.width <= width) {

content.text:
Ah — yes, that reading makes more sense, and I think it's a good call. `pageCache.ts` already establishes exactly this idiom: module-scope `Map`s/flags instead of refs, a `notify()`/`subscribe()` pair, and a thin `usePageCacheRender()` hook that just forces a re-render tick on notify. Doing the same for the upload queue would replace `jobsRef`/`pendingRef`/`runningRef`/`cancelledRef`/`genRef` with plain top-level `let`/`const` variables — the mutex-like guards (`runningRef`, `cancelledRef`, `genRef`) stop being an awkward fit for React's re-render model and become just... normal synchronous variables, which is what they conceptually are. It'd also make the queue logic testable as plain async functions without `renderHook`/`act` ceremony.

The one thing I'd need to add that `pageCache` doesn't have: an explicit reset/clear, since module state persists for the life of the page and needs to be wiped both between test cases and when the user picks a new root folder (per the spec's "discards the whole tree and upload-queue state" requirement) — `pageCache` gets away without one because `evict()` is scoped per-path, not a full-queue wipe.

Given the precedent already exists in this codebase and the queue is genuinely single-instance, I'd switch to it. Want me to redo `useUploadQueue` this way before we commit 6a?

input.content:
Add Drive Upload Step 6a: upload queue state model + backend RPC

uploadQueue tracks per-file status (idle/queued/uploading/done/error) via
a sequential (concurrency=1) worker. It's a module-level singleton
(matching lib/pageCache's pattern) rather than a hook: there is only ever
one upload run in flight for the app, so its lifetime doesn't need to be
tied to a component instance, and the mutex/generation-counter bookkeeping
the worker needs maps onto plain module variables far more naturally than
onto refs fighting React's render model. Callers pass in pre-resolved jobs
(path/folderId/name) rather than the module knowing about the file tree or
Drive assignments itself.

flattenFiles(group) is the shared tree-traversal utility the worker, the
upload modal's rollup counts, and the Open-in-Drive check will all reuse
instead of drifting apart.

drive.UploadFile gains a name parameter (defaulting to the local
basename) so its signature won't need to change again once inline
renaming (Step 4) lands; App.UploadFile wraps it as a Wails RPC.

No UI yet — that's Step 6b (modal) and 6c (Upload All button, read-only
lock, post-run badges).

content.content:
1	import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
2	import { UploadFile } from '../../../wailsjs/go/main/App'
3	
4	export type UploadStatus = 'idle' | 'queued' | 'uploading' | 'done' | 'error'
5	
6	export interface UploadFileState {
7	  status: UploadStatus
8	  error?: string
9	}
10	
11	export interface UploadJob {
12	  path: string
13	  folderId: string
14	  name: string
15	}
16	
17	// Per-file upload status, driven by a sequential (concurrency = 1) worker.
18	// A module-level singleton (like ../../lib/pageCache) rather than a hook:
19	// there is only ever one upload run in flight for the app, so the queue's
20	// lifetime doesn't need to be tied to any one component instance. Callers
21	// resolve each file's destination folder/name up front and pass in an
22	// ordered list of jobs — this module only knows how to run them one at a
23	// time and track status, not about the file tree or Drive assignments.
24	const statusByPath = new Map<string, UploadFileState>()
25	const jobByPath = new Map<string, UploadJob>()
26	const pendingPaths: string[] = []
27	const listeners = new Set<() => void>()
28	let running = false
29	let cancelled = false
30	// Bumped by reset() so a job that was already in flight can't write a
31	// stale status back in after the run it belonged to was wiped.
32	let generation = 0
33	
34	function notify() {
35	  for (const fn of listeners) fn()
36	}
37	
38	export function subscribe(fn: () => void): () => void {
39	  listeners.add(fn)
40	  return () => listeners.delete(fn)
41	}
42	
43	export function useUploadQueueRender() {
44	  const [, setTick] = useState(0)
45	  useEffect(() => subscribe(() => setTick(t => t + 1)), [])
46	}
47	
48	export function getStatus(path: string): UploadFileState | undefined {
49	  return statusByPath.get(path)
50	}
51	
52	function setStatus(path: string, state: UploadFileState) {
53	  statusByPath.set(path, state)
54	  notify()
55	}
56	
57	async function runQueue(gen: number) {
58	  if (running) return
59	  running = true
60	  while (!cancelled && generation === gen && pendingPaths.length > 0) {
61	    const path = pendingPaths.shift()!
62	    const job = jobByPath.get(path)
63	    if (!job) continue
64	    setStatus(path, { status: 'uploading' })
65	    try {
66	      await UploadFile(job.path, job.folderId, job.name)
67	      if (generation !== gen) break
68	      setStatus(path, { status: 'done' })
69	    } catch (e) {
70	      if (generation !== gen) break
71	      setStatus(path, { status: 'error', error: String(e) })
72	    }
73	  }
74	  running = false
75	}
76	
77	function enqueue(newJobs: UploadJob[]) {
78	  if (newJobs.length === 0) return
79	  cancelled = false
80	  for (const job of newJobs) {
81	    jobByPath.set(job.path, job)
82	    pendingPaths.push(job.path)
83	    statusByPath.set(job.path, { status: 'queued' })
84	  }
85	  notify()
86	  void runQueue(generation)
87	}
88	
89	export function start(newJobs: UploadJob[]): void {
90	  enqueue(newJobs)
91	}
92	
93	export function retry(job: UploadJob): void {
94	  enqueue([job])
95	}
96	
97	// Stops starting new files; does not abort an in-flight request. Files
98	// still waiting their turn go back to idle since they were never attempted.
99	export function cancelRemaining(): void {
100	  cancelled = true
101	  const skipped = pendingPaths.splice(0, pendingPaths.length)
102	  for (const path of skipped) statusByPath.set(path, { status: 'idle' })
103	  notify()
104	}
105	
106	export function reset(): void {
107	  generation += 1
108	  cancelled = true
109	  jobByPath.clear()
110	  pendingPaths.splice(0, pendingPaths.length)
111	  statusByPath.clear()
112	  notify()
113	}

message.content: Line 63 says: `if (!job) continue`. When does it happen that job is empty?

content.text:
Good catch — let me trace it: `pendingPaths` and `jobByPath` are only ever written together. `enqueue()` is the only place that pushes onto `pendingPaths`, and it always does `jobByPath.set(job.path, job)` in the same loop iteration, before the push. Nothing ever deletes a single entry from `jobByPath` — `reset()` is the only thing that clears it, and `reset()` clears `pendingPaths` in the same call, so a stale path can't survive into the next loop iteration under a still-valid `generation`. `cancelRemaining()` empties `pendingPaths` but doesn't touch `jobByPath`, which just leaves harmless orphaned entries, not the reverse (a `pendingPaths` entry with no `jobByPath` counterpart).

So under the invariants this module actually maintains, `job` can never be `undefined` there — I added it as a defensive guard without a real scenario behind it, which isn't something I should've included per the project's guidance against handling cases that can't happen. I'd rather make the invariant explicit the same way line 61 already does (`pendingPaths.shift()!`):

```ts
const path = pendingPaths.shift()!
const job = jobByPath.get(path)!
```

Want me to make that change?

message.content: `const skipped = pendingPaths.splice(0, pendingPaths.length)` clears the array, right? Wouldn't it be easier to just do `const skipped = []`? Same for all the other similar cases.

content.text:
`splice(0, pendingPaths.length)` does two things at once: it empties the array *and* returns everything that was in it. In `cancelRemaining()` that return value is exactly what's needed — `skipped` is iterated right after to revert those files' status to `idle`, so it can't just be `[]`; we need the actual paths that were pending.

`reset()` is a different story — there the return value is discarded, so `splice` is doing more work than needed just to clear the array. That one should be `pendingPaths.length = 0`, which is the idiomatic in-place array clear (arrays don't have `.clear()` the way `Map` does, which is why `jobByPath.clear()`/`statusByPath.clear()` look different right next to it).

message.content: In cancelRemaining() you could first loop through pending and reset it afterward. What's the reason to reset all these variables in place? Why not just assign a new value? I'm asking because for Array.splice() and [].length = 0 it's not immediately clear what the purpose is, at least not compared to a simple assignment.

content.text:
Good question — there's no real reason. These are module-scope `const` bindings, but nothing outside this module ever gets a direct reference to the `pendingPaths` array or the `statusByPath`/`jobByPath` maps (the only public accessor is `getStatus(path)`, which reads one value at a time). Since nothing aliases them, there's no requirement to preserve object identity — reassignment is just as correct as mutation, and it doesn't force the reader to already know that `splice(0, len)` or `.length = 0` are ways to empty an array in place.

I'll switch `pendingPaths` (and `jobByPath`/`statusByPath` for consistency) from `const` to `let` and reassign instead:

1	import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
2	import { UploadFile } from '../../../wailsjs/go/main/App'
3	
4	export type UploadStatus = 'idle' | 'queued' | 'uploading' | 'done' | 'error'
5	
6	export interface UploadFileState {
7	  status: UploadStatus
8	  error?: string
9	}
10	
11	export interface UploadJob {
12	  path: string
13	  folderId: string
14	  name: string
15	}
16	
17	// Per-file upload status, driven by a sequential (concurrency = 1) worker.
18	// A module-level singleton (like ../../lib/pageCache) rather than a hook:
19	// there is only ever one upload run in flight for the app, so the queue's
20	// lifetime doesn't need to be tied to any one component instance. Callers
21	// resolve each file's destination folder/name up front and pass in an
22	// ordered list of jobs — this module only knows how to run them one at a
23	// time and track status, not about the file tree or Drive assignments.
24	const statusByPath = new Map<string, UploadFileState>()
25	const jobByPath = new Map<string, UploadJob>()
26	const pendingPaths: string[] = []
27	const listeners = new Set<() => void>()
28	let running = false
29	let cancelled = false
30	// Bumped by reset() so a job that was already in flight can't write a
31	// stale status back in after the run it belonged to was wiped.
32	let generation = 0
33	
34	function notify() {
35	  for (const fn of listeners) fn()
36	}
37	
38	export function subscribe(fn: () => void): () => void {
39	  listeners.add(fn)
40	  return () => listeners.delete(fn)
41	}
42	
43	export function useUploadQueueRender() {
44	  const [, setTick] = useState(0)
45	  useEffect(() => subscribe(() => setTick(t => t + 1)), [])
46	}
47	
48	export function getStatus(path: string): UploadFileState | undefined {
49	  return statusByPath.get(path)
50	}
51	
52	function setStatus(path: string, state: UploadFileState) {
53	  statusByPath.set(path, state)
54	  notify()
55	}
56	
57	async function runQueue(gen: number) {
58	  if (running) return
59	  running = true
60	  while (!cancelled && generation === gen && pendingPaths.length > 0) {
61	    const path = pendingPaths.shift()!
62	    const job = jobByPath.get(path)!
63	    setStatus(path, { status: 'uploading' })
64	    try {
65	      await UploadFile(job.path, job.folderId, job.name)
66	      if (generation !== gen) break
67	      setStatus(path, { status: 'done' })
68	    } catch (e) {
69	      if (generation !== gen) break
70	      setStatus(path, { status: 'error', error: String(e) })
71	    }
72	  }
73	  running = false
74	}
75	
76	function enqueue(newJobs: UploadJob[]) {
77	  if (newJobs.length === 0) return
78	  cancelled = false
79	  for (const job of newJobs) {
80	    jobByPath.set(job.path, job)
81	    pendingPaths.push(job.path)
82	    statusByPath.set(job.path, { status: 'queued' })
83	  }
84	  notify()
85	  void runQueue(generation)
86	}
87	
88	export function start(newJobs: UploadJob[]): void {
89	  enqueue(newJobs)
90	}
91	
92	export function retry(job: UploadJob): void {
93	  enqueue([job])
94	}
95	
96	// Stops starting new files; does not abort an in-flight request. Files
97	// still waiting their turn go back to idle since they were never attempted.
98	export function cancelRemaining(): void {
99	  cancelled = true
100	  const skipped = pendingPaths.splice(0, pendingPaths.length)
101	  for (const path of skipped) statusByPath.set(path, { status: 'idle' })
102	  notify()
103	}
104	
105	export function reset(): void {
106	  generation += 1
107	  cancelled = true
108	  jobByPath.clear()
109	  pendingPaths.length = 0
110	  statusByPath.clear()
111	  notify()
112	}

message.content: How about merging UploadFileState and UploadJob?

content.text:
Yes, that's a good simplification — it removes the exact problem your earlier question was circling: two parallel `Map`s (`jobByPath`, `statusByPath`) that have to be kept in sync by construction. One merged type means one `Map`, and the "does every pending path have a job" invariant disappears because there's only one thing to look up.

One naming snag: I can't call the merged type `UploadFile`, since that's already the name of the imported RPC function (`import { UploadFile } from '.../App'`). TS would technically allow it (types and values live in separate namespaces) but it'd be confusing to read. I'd call it `UploadEntry`:

```ts
export interface UploadJob {
  path: string
  folderId: string
  name: string
}

export interface UploadEntry extends UploadJob {
  status: UploadStatus
  error?: string
}
```

`filesByPath: Map<string, UploadEntry>` replaces both maps. The one tradeoff: every status transition needs to spread the existing entry to keep its `path`/`folderId`/`name` (`{ ...existing, status: 'uploading' }`) rather than the current one-liner (`{ status: 'uploading' }`) — I'd pull that into a small `updateStatus(path, patch)` helper so it's not repeated four times.

Want me to make this change?

content.text:
You're right — this is a real gap, and not a "can't happen" one. Trace it: `retry(job: UploadJob)` → `enqueue([job])` → `filesByPath.set(job.path, { ...job, status: 'queued' })`. That only clears `.error` if `job` is *structurally* a bare `{path, folderId, name}`. But `UploadEntry extends UploadJob`, so it's structurally assignable — and the natural way 6b's Retry button will call this is by passing the `UploadEntry` it already has from `getStatus(path)` (rather than reconstructing a fresh `UploadJob`). TypeScript won't flag that (excess-property checks only apply to object literals, not to a variable of a wider type), and at runtime that object still carries its old `.status: 'error'` / `.error: '...'` fields — which the spread would carry into the new "queued" entry, since only `status` is explicitly overridden.

Fix: explicitly clear `error` too, not just `status`.

input.old_string: filesByPath.set(job.path, { ...job, status: 'queued' })
input.new_string: filesByPath.set(job.path, { ...job, status: 'queued', error: undefined })

content.text:
Confirmed and fixed. Summary:

- `enqueue()` now explicitly clears `error: undefined` when building the `'queued'` entry, so `retry()` can't leak a stale error through — this mattered because `UploadEntry` is structurally assignable to `UploadJob` (it's a superset), so passing the `UploadEntry` a Retry button already has (rather than a hand-trimmed `UploadJob`) type-checks fine but previously carried the old `.error` through the spread.
- Added a regression test that reproduces the realistic call site (`retry(staleEntry)` where `staleEntry` is a full `UploadEntry`) and verifies `.error` is cleared. I confirmed it actually catches the bug by reverting the fix and watching it fail, then restored the fix.

One side note from building that test: I had to keep the queue "busy" on a second file to observe the requeued entry before it flips to `'uploading'` (which would've cleared `.error` on its own and masked the bug). While doing that I noticed `reset()` doesn't clear the `running` flag, so a `reset()` fired while a request is genuinely stuck in flight would wedge the queue for good. I didn't fix that — per the spec, `reset()` can only happen via picking a new root folder, and the upload modal's full-viewport overlay blocks that button for the entire time anything could be in flight, so the scenario isn't reachable through the actual UI (same reasoning as the singleton question earlier). Flagging in case you'd rather harden it anyway.

Typecheck and all 29 tests pass.

content.text:
Here's the full list, in order:

1. **Why all the `useRef`s in `useUploadQueue`?** — Explained (mutex/queue/generation bookkeeping needs synchronous read/write across an async closure that `useState` can't provide). No code change.
2. **Would `useEffectEvent()` fit better than refs?** — Explained no: it only works for reading fresh state from *inside* an Effect, and there's no Effect here — the run loop is triggered by plain callbacks. No code change.
3. **Isn't the queue basically a singleton — why not a real one instead of hooks?** — Led into #4 once clarified.
4. **Clarified: module-level variables, like `pageCache`** — Rewrote `useUploadQueue` (a hook with refs) into `uploadQueue.ts`, a module-level singleton matching `lib/pageCache.ts`'s `subscribe`/`notify` pattern.
5. **Map keys (`statuses`, `jobs`) weren't self-documenting — just typed `string`** — Renamed to `statusByPath` / `jobByPath` / `pendingPaths`.
6. **`if (!job) continue` — when does that actually happen?** — Traced the invariants and found it can't happen; removed the guard, used a `!` non-null assertion instead (`jobByPath.get(path)!`).
7. **`pendingPaths.splice(0, pendingPaths.length)` clears the array — could it just be `const skipped = []`?** — Clarified: `cancelRemaining()` needs the removed items, so `splice` stays there; `reset()` doesn't use the return value, so simplified to `pendingPaths.length = 0`.
8. **Why mutate in place (`splice`/`.length = 0`) instead of reassigning?** — No aliasing requires mutation, so switched `pendingPaths` from `const` to `let` and reassigned (`pendingPaths = []`) in both `cancelRemaining()` and `reset()`. Left `Map.clear()` as-is since it's already self-descriptive.
9. **Merge `UploadFileState` and `UploadJob`?** — Merged into one `UploadEntry` type, collapsing the two parallel `Map`s (`jobByPath` + `statusByPath`) into one `filesByPath`, with an `updateStatus()` helper.
10. **Why `const skipped = pendingPaths` before looping, instead of looping directly?** — No reason (leftover from the earlier `splice`-based shape); simplified `cancelRemaining()` to loop over `pendingPaths` directly, then reassign after.
11. **"Now merge the actual types"** — Collapsed `UploadJob`/`UploadEntry` further into one canonical interface with `UploadJob = Omit<UploadEntry, 'status' | 'error'>`.
12. **"No, go back to the previous version"** — Reverted #11, back to `UploadEntry extends UploadJob`.
13. **Shouldn't `retry()` clear the `.error` field?** — Found a real bug: since `UploadEntry` is structurally assignable to `UploadJob`, a Retry button passing back the stale `UploadEntry` it already has would leak the old `.error` through `enqueue()`'s spread. Fixed by explicitly setting `error: undefined`; added a regression test that reproduces the realistic call site and confirmed it catches the bug when reverted.
14. **"Let's clear `running`"** — Fixed `reset()` to not leave `running` stuck `true` behind an abandoned in-flight request; made `runQueue`'s own cleanup generation-aware (`if (generation === gen) running = false`) so a late-settling abandoned request can't clobber a newer legitimate run. Added a regression test covering the full sequence.
15. **Shouldn't `reset()`'s `cancelled` be `false`, not `true`, to match the initial state?** — Confirmed `true` was never load-bearing (the `generation` check alone already stops an abandoned loop) and changed it to `false` for accurate "pristine state" semantics.

Net effect: `useUploadQueue.ts` → `uploadQueue.ts` (module singleton), two `Map`s → one, `UploadJob`/`UploadEntry` as a clean two-interface pair, one real bug fixed (stale `.error` on retry) and one real bug fixed (`running` wedging across `reset()`), both with regression tests, plus several dead-code/naming/idiom cleanups.

input.content:
Add Drive Upload Step 6a: upload queue state model + backend RPC

uploadQueue tracks per-file status (idle/queued/uploading/done/error) via
a sequential (concurrency=1) worker. It's a module-level singleton
(matching lib/pageCache's pattern) rather than a hook: there is only ever
one upload run in flight for the app, so its lifetime doesn't need to be
tied to a component instance, and the mutex/generation-counter bookkeeping
the worker needs maps onto plain module variables far more naturally than
onto refs fighting React's render model. Callers pass in pre-resolved jobs
(path/folderId/name) rather than the module knowing about the file tree or
Drive assignments itself; status and destination are merged into one
UploadEntry per path rather than two parallel maps that would need to be
kept in sync.

Two correctness fixes worth calling out:
- retry() explicitly clears the previous .error when requeuing, since
  UploadEntry is structurally assignable to UploadJob — a Retry button
  passing back the UploadEntry it already has (rather than a hand-trimmed
  UploadJob) would otherwise leak the old error through.
- reset() clears the `running` flag, and runQueue()'s own cleanup only
  clears it if it's still cleaning up for the current generation. Without
  this, resetting while a request is genuinely stuck in flight would wedge
  the queue: the abandoned request settling later would either block a
  fresh run from starting, or clobber one that already had.

flattenFiles(group) is the shared tree-traversal utility the worker, the
upload modal's rollup counts, and the Open-in-Drive check will all reuse
instead of drifting apart.

drive.UploadFile now requires a non-empty name and errors instead of
falling back to the local basename — the frontend always supplies one, so
a silent fallback would only hide a real bug. App.UploadFile wraps it as
a Wails RPC.

No UI yet — that's Step 6b (modal) and 6c (Upload All button, read-only
lock, post-run badges).

12	// UploadFile uploads the local file at localPath to the Drive folder with

14	// Returns the ID of the created Drive file.
15	func UploadFile(ctx context.Context, localPath, folderID string) (string, error) {
16		f, err := os.Open(localPath)
17		if err != nil {
18			return "", fmt.Errorf("open %s: %w", localPath, err)
19		}
20		defer f.Close()
21	
22		svc, err := service(ctx)
23		if err != nil {
24			return "", err
25		}
26	
27		meta := &drive.File{
28			Name:    filepath.Base(localPath),
29			Parents: []string{folderID},
30		}
31		created, err := svc.Files.Create(meta).Media(f).Fields("id, name, size").Do()
32		if err != nil {
33			return "", fmt.Errorf("upload %s: %w", localPath, err)
34		}
35		return created.Id, nil
36	}

1	# Paper Scan Processor
2	
3	A desktop application for post-processing PDF files containing batches of scanned documents. The app has three modes: **Merge**, **Split**, and **Drive Upload**.
4	
5	## Tech stack
6	
7	- **Desktop framework**: Wails
8	- **Backend**: Go
9	- **Frontend**: TypeScript + React
10	- **UI components**: Mantine
11	- **Virtualization**: TanStack Virtual
12	- **Drag-and-drop**: dnd-kit
13	- **PDF manipulation**: pdfcpu
14	- **PDF rendering** (thumbnails): `pdftoppm` (Poppler, system install, called as subprocess)
15	
16	## Common elements
17	
18	Both modes include a thumbnail panel and a page detail panel, and support the same per-page editing operations.
19	
20	### Thumbnail panel
21	
22	A vertically scrolling strip of page thumbnails. Width is user-adjustable via a drag handle; thumbnails scale to fill the panel width. Rendering is on-demand and virtualized — only visible thumbnails (plus a small overscan buffer) are rendered at any given time.
23	
24	The Go backend exposes a per-page render method returning a base64-encoded PNG; the frontend requests thumbnails as they scroll into view (`pdftoppm` subprocess).
25	
26	#### Keyboard shortcuts
27	
28	| Key                    | Action                                     |
29	| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
30	| `R`                    | Rotate selected page clockwise 90°         |
31	| `Shift+R`              | Rotate selected page counter-clockwise 90° |
32	| `Delete` / `Backspace` | Toggle skip on the selected page           |
33	| `←` / `→`              | Select previous / next page                |
34	
35	### Page detail panel
36	
37	Shows the currently selected page at reading resolution. Selecting a thumbnail updates it.
38	
39	Supports:
40	
41	- **Pan**: drag to pan.
42	- **Zoom**: scroll wheel or trackpad pinch to zoom in/out.
43	- **Navigate**: `←` / `→` to move to the previous/next page.
44	
45	Implemented with `react-zoom-pan-pinch`.
46	
47	### Page editing
48	
49	Individual pages can be edited in both modes before export or merge:
50	
51	- **Rotation**: pages can be rotated in 90° increments (clockwise or counter-clockwise).
52	- **Skip**: pages can be marked as skipped — excluded from the output but remaining visible in the thumbnail view (greyed out). A page is skipped by clicking a skip icon that appears on hover, or via keyboard shortcut.
53	- **Reorder**: pages can be reordered by dragging thumbnails to a new position.
54	
55	## Mode: Merge
56	
57	For scanners that can only scan one side at a time. The user scans all front pages as one PDF and all back pages as another, then uses Merge mode to interleave them into a single PDF.
58	
59	### Workflow
60	
61	1. The user loads two PDF files, labelled **File A** and **File B**.
62	2. The user selects which file contains the first page (**First page in: File A / File B**).
63	3. A **Reverse File B** checkbox controls whether File B is reversed before interleaving. This should be checked when the paper stack was flipped between scans (the typical case, when scanning one side at a time), causing the second-scanned pages to be in reverse order.
64	4. The app interleaves the pages: A1, B1, A2, B2, etc.
65	5. The user saves the merged result as a new PDF file on disk.
66	
67	The merged PDF can then be opened in Split mode for further processing.
68	
69	### Unequal page counts
70	
71	If File A and File B have different page counts, the app shows a warning before proceeding: "File A has X pages, File B has Y pages. The extra Z page(s) will be appended at the end." The user can cancel or continue. The extra pages from the longer file are appended in order after the interleaved section.
72	
73	### Layout
74	
75	Merge mode uses a two-column layout:
76	
77	- **Left panel** — two side-by-side thumbnail strips, one per input file.
78	- **Right panel** (fills remaining space) — the page detail view, showing whichever page was most recently selected in either thumbnail strip.
79	
80	The thumbnail strip for the file containing the second output page is offset downward by half a thumbnail height. This makes the interleaving order visually apparent: the two files' pages appear to slot between each other.
81	
82	```
83	  A               B
84	  ┌──────────┐
85	  │   A1     │
86	  └──────────┘  ┌──────────┐
87	                │   B1     │
88	  ┌──────────┐  └──────────┘
89	  │   A2     │
90	  └──────────┘  ┌──────────┐
91	                │   B2     │
92	  ┌──────────┐  └──────────┘
93	  │   A3     │
94	  └──────────┘
95	```
96	
97	The offset makes the interleaving order visually apparent without needing labels.
98	
99	### Error handling
100	
101	TBD.
102	
103	## Mode: Split
104	
105	### Workflow
106	
107	1. The user loads an input PDF via a file picker dialog or by dragging and dropping a file onto the app window.
108	2. The app displays all pages as thumbnails in the left panel. Clicking a thumbnail selects it and updates the detail panel on the right.
109	3. The user defines split points by clicking in the gaps between page thumbnails. A visual divider appears at each split point; clicking again removes it. Dividers can also be repositioned by dragging them to a different gap. Each divider marks where a new output file begins.
110	4. The user sets a global filename template using `{date}` (today's date as `YYYY-MM-DD`) and `{name}` (a per-file label). Example: `{date} {name}` → `2026-06-12 invoice.pdf`. The app prefills the filename for each output file using this template. The user can then edit any individual file's name before exporting.
111	5. The user sets a global output folder (an existing folder on the local filesystem). For each output file, the user can adjust:
112	   - The prefilled filename (editable)
113	   - The destination folder (overridable per file)
114	6. The user clicks Export. Before splitting, the app checks for filename conflicts at each destination. If any conflict is found, the export is aborted and an error message identifies the conflicting files. Once resolved, the app splits the input PDF and writes each output file. Afterwards, the app prompts the user to keep, move, or delete the input file. The success modal includes an **"Open in Drive Upload"** button that switches to Drive Upload mode with the output folder pre-set as the root.
115	
116	### Layout
117	
118	Split mode uses a two-column layout:
119	
120	- **Left panel** (adjustable width, drag handle on right edge) — a single vertically scrolling area that combines the thumbnail strip and output file controls.
121	- **Right panel** (fills remaining space) — the page detail view.
122	
123	#### Left panel structure
124	
125	The left panel is a continuous scroll area. Pages are grouped by output file. Each group is preceded by a compact **output file header** containing the editable filename field and (when applicable) destination folder. Split-point dividers between groups are the visual boundary between one output file and the next.
126	
127	```
128	┌─ invoice.pdf ──────────────────────┐
129	│ folder: /Documents                 │
130	└────────────────────────────────────┘
131	  [page 1 thumbnail]
132	  [page 2 thumbnail]
133	  [page 3 thumbnail]
134	  ──────── [gap / split point] ───────
135	┌─ receipt.pdf ──────────────────────┐
136	│ folder: /Documents                 │
137	└────────────────────────────────────┘
138	  [page 4 thumbnail]
139	  [page 5 thumbnail]
140	```
141	
142	Clicking a gap toggles a split point there and creates a new output file section. The filename and folder fields for each section appear immediately above its pages.
143	
144	### Keyboard shortcuts
145	
146	| Key     | Action                                                  |
147	| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
148	| `Space` | Toggle a split point after the selected page            |
149	| `Tab`   | Move focus to the next filename input in the left panel |
150
